## Overview

This project explores **binary credit risk classification** using the `credit_data` dataset from the R package `modeldata`. The goal is to predict whether a customer belongs to the `bad` or `good` credit status class.

The study compares **logistic regression** and **Random Forest** under three preprocessing strategies, for a total of six model configurations. Beyond overall accuracy, the analysis considers how effectively the models identify customers in the higher-risk (`bad`) class.

## Libraries

The analysis uses the R tidyverse and tidymodels ecosystem for data exploration, preprocessing, resampling, model fitting and evaluation.

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| label: load-packages

library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(modeldata)
library(skimr)
library(vip)

library(rsample)
library(recipes)
library(parsnip)
library(workflows)
library(workflowsets)
library(dials)
library(tune)
library(yardstick)

# silniki modeli wykorzystane w workflow_set:
library(ranger)
library(glmnet)
```

## Dataset Overview

The dataset contains **4,454 observations**. Initial inspection provides an overview of feature types and data completeness.

```{r}
data(credit_data)
skim(credit_data)
```

### Data Preview

```{r}
credit_data
```

### Missing-Value Assessment

Several variables contain missing values, particularly `Income`. Instead of discarding incomplete records, missing-value handling is included in the model recipes.

```{r}
colSums(is.na(credit_data))
cat("Rows with at least one missing value:", 
    sum(rowSums(is.na(credit_data)) > 0), "\n")
```

### Target Distribution

The target variable `Status` contains **1,254 `bad`** and **3,200 `good`** observations. This class imbalance makes accuracy alone an incomplete performance measure.

In `yardstick`, the first factor level (`bad`) is treated as the event by default. Accordingly, sensitivity measures the detection of `bad` cases, while specificity measures the correct recognition of `good` cases.

```{r}
table(credit_data$Status)
prop.table(table(credit_data$Status)) %>% round(3)
levels(credit_data$Status)
```

## Training and Test Sets

A **70/30 stratified split** preserves the distribution of `Status` across the training and held-out test sets.

```{r}
set.seed(347793)
podzial <- initial_split(credit_data, prop = 0.70, strata = Status)

train_data <- training(podzial)
test_data  <- testing(podzial)

cat("Training set:", nrow(train_data), "obserwacji\n")
cat("Test set:   ", nrow(test_data), "obserwacji\n")

cat("\nStatus proportions (training):\n")
print(prop.table(table(train_data$Status)) %>% round(3))
cat("\nStatus proportions (test):\n")
print(prop.table(table(test_data$Status)) %>% round(3))
```

## Preprocessing

Three strategies are compared:

- **Recipe 1:** Imputation, dummy encoding and normalization using all predictors.
- **Recipe 2:** The same general inputs plus financial ratios, grouping of infrequent categorical levels and removal of highly correlated numeric features.
- **Recipe 3:** A reduced, domain-motivated selection of predictors.

Defining these operations in `recipes` allows preprocessing to be estimated within each training fold.

```{r}
# Przepis 1: wszystkie zmienne, "standardowe" przygotowanie danych
# (imputacja braków, kodowanie zmiennych kategorycznych, standaryzacja)
rec_1 <- recipe(Status ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

# Przepis 2: wszystkie zmienne + dodatkowe zmienne pochodne 
# (wskaźniki finansowe: zadłużenie/dochód, majątek/dochód, kwota/dochód),
# rzadkie poziomy zmiennych kategorycznych grupowane w "pozostałe",
# a silnie skorelowane zmienne liczbowe usuwane
rec_2 <- recipe(Status ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_mutate(
    Debt_Income   = Debt / (Income + 1),
    Assets_Income = Assets / (Income + 1),
    Amount_Income = Amount / (Income + 1)
  ) %>%
  step_other(Home, Marital, Job, threshold = 0.05, other = "pozostale") %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_corr(all_numeric_predictors(), threshold = 0.9)

# Przepis 3: ograniczony, "ekspercki" zestaw zmiennych - tylko te, które
# intuicyjnie powinny mieć największe znaczenie dla oceny zdolności kredytowej
rec_3 <- recipe(Status ~ Seniority + Home + Records + Job + Income + Assets + Debt + Amount,
                data = train_data) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
```

## Model Specifications

The analysis compares a Random Forest classifier (`ranger`) and logistic regression (`glm`).

```{r}
model_rf <- rand_forest() %>%
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 347793, importance = "permutation") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

model_log <- logistic_reg() %>%
  set_engine("glm") %>%
  set_mode("classification")
```

### Candidate Workflows

The three recipes and two model specifications are combined into **six workflows** for consistent comparison.

```{r}
zestaw_workflow <- workflow_set(
  preproc = list(rec_1 = rec_1, rec_2 = rec_2, rec_3 = rec_3),
  models  = list(model_rf = model_rf, model_log = model_log),
  cross   = TRUE
)
zestaw_workflow
```

## Cross-Validation

Five-fold stratified cross-validation is used on the training set to evaluate the candidate workflows.

```{r}
#| label: cross-validation-folds

set.seed(347793)
foldy <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5, strata = Status)
foldy
```

### Model Training

The workflows are evaluated using accuracy, ROC AUC, sensitivity and specificity. Particular attention is given to sensitivity for the `bad` class, since missed high-risk cases may be consequential in a lending context.

```{r}
#| label: train-candidate-models
#| cache: true

zbior_metryk <- metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc, sens, spec)

set.seed(347793)
wyniki_cv <- zestaw_workflow %>%
  workflow_map(
    "fit_resamples",
    resamples = foldy,
    metrics   = zbior_metryk,
    control   = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE),
    seed      = 347793,
    verbose   = TRUE
  )
```

### Cross-Validation Results

The recorded results indicate that **`rec_1_model_log`** has the highest accuracy (approximately **0.796**), while **`rec_2_model_rf`** has the highest ROC AUC (approximately **0.834**). The top AUC scores are very close.

For the accuracy-leading model, sensitivity for `bad` customers is approximately **0.50**, versus specificity of approximately **0.91**. This illustrates why selecting a credit risk classifier solely on accuracy can be misleading.

These values refer to the original run and should be checked again if the experiment is rerun with different settings.

## Held-Out Test Evaluation

The highest-ranked workflow by cross-validation accuracy is refitted and evaluated on the test set, which was not used to compare candidate workflows.

```{r}
tabela_wynikow <- collect_metrics(wyniki_cv) %>%
  select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = c(mean, std_err)) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_accuracy))

tabela_wynikow
```

### Confusion Matrix

The confusion matrix helps distinguish the different types of classification errors, especially high-risk customers classified as `good`.

```{r}
najlepszy_id <- rank_results(wyniki_cv, rank_metric = "accuracy", select_best = FALSE) %>%
  filter(.metric == "accuracy") %>%
  arrange(rank) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  pull(wflow_id)

najlepszy_id

najlepszy_workflow <- extract_workflow(wyniki_cv, najlepszy_id)

set.seed(347793)
finalny_fit <- last_fit(najlepszy_workflow, split = podzial,
                         metrics = metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc, sens, spec))

cat("--- Test set metrics ---\n")
collect_metrics(finalny_fit)
```

## Feature Importance

The best Random Forest and logistic regression configurations are selected by cross-validation accuracy and refitted to the training set to examine influential predictors.

```{r}
predykcje_testowe <- collect_predictions(finalny_fit)

cat("--- Test set confusion matrix ---\n")
conf_mat(predykcje_testowe, truth = Status, estimate = .pred_class)
```

### Selecting Models for Interpretation

The top-performing configuration from each model family is selected using cross-validation accuracy.

```{r}
# najlepszy model Random Forest oraz najlepszy model regresji logistycznej
# (wg dokładności w kroswalidacji)
najlepszy_rf_id  <- collect_metrics(wyniki_cv) %>% 
  filter(.metric == "accuracy", str_detect(wflow_id, "model_rf")) %>% 
  arrange(desc(mean)) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(wflow_id)

najlepszy_log_id <- collect_metrics(wyniki_cv) %>% 
  filter(.metric == "accuracy", str_detect(wflow_id, "model_log")) %>% 
  arrange(desc(mean)) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(wflow_id)

cat("Best Random Forest: ", najlepszy_rf_id,  "\n")
cat("Best logistic regression: ", najlepszy_log_id, "\n")

wf_rf  <- extract_workflow(wyniki_cv, najlepszy_rf_id)
wf_log <- extract_workflow(wyniki_cv, najlepszy_log_id)

set.seed(347793)
fit_rf  <- fit(wf_rf,  data = train_data)
set.seed(347793)
fit_log <- fit(wf_log, data = train_data)
```

### Importance Plots

The plots provide model-specific views of feature importance. Their values should not be interpreted as directly comparable across algorithms.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6

library(patchwork)

p_rf <- vip(extract_fit_parsnip(fit_rf), num_features = 10, geom = "col") +
  labs(title = "Feature importance - Random Forest", subtitle = najlepszy_rf_id) +
  theme_minimal()

p_log <- vip(extract_fit_parsnip(fit_log), num_features = 10, geom = "col") +
  labs(title = "Feature importance - Logistic Regression", subtitle = najlepszy_log_id) +
  theme_minimal()

p_rf + p_log
```

## Discussion

The original analysis identifies **employment seniority, previous credit records, income and loan amount** among the influential predictors. Rankings differ across models.

The results illustrate that high ROC AUC does not necessarily imply high sensitivity at the default classification threshold. Class weighting, threshold adjustment and additional validation are possible future directions, **not experiments performed here**.

## Limitations and Reproducibility

This is an **educational modelling study**, not a validated credit decision system. The dataset is loaded from `modeldata`; no external CSV is required.

**Before publication:** The original code uses `347793` (a student identifier) as its random seed. It has been preserved to avoid changing the recorded experiment. Replace it with a neutral seed, rerun the analysis, and update reported values if they change.
